questions.q: What is a highlight table, structurally?
options: A text table (rows and columns of categories) with a measure mapped to Color, so cell color surfaces the pattern instead of requiring you to scan every number
A bar chart with highlighted axis labels
A map with highlighted country borders
A pie chart where one slice is visually separated from the rest
questions.explain: A highlight table keeps the readable grid structure of a plain text table while using color, driven by a measure, to make the pattern jump out visually.

questions.q: What single change turns a highlight table into a heat map?
options: Adding a second measure to Size, so cell size varies alongside cell color
Switching the mark type from Square to Circle
Removing all dimensions from Rows
Changing the color palette from orange to blue
questions.explain: A heat map is a highlight table plus a second measure encoded via Size — the color still shows one measure while size now shows another.

questions.q: Why does a diverging color palette suit a measure like Profit better than a sequential one?
options: Because Profit can be negative or positive, and a diverging palette ramps two different colors toward each extreme, meeting at a neutral midpoint at zero
Because diverging palettes always render faster than sequential ones
Because Profit is always a whole number
Sequential palettes cannot be applied to any measure in Tableau
questions.explain: A diverging palette is built for measures that can swing negative or positive, unlike a sequential palette which is better suited to always-positive measures like Sales or Quantity.

questions.q: What does adding a medium-gray border to each cell accomplish in a highlight table?
options: It makes individual cells easier to distinguish from similarly colored neighbors
It converts the highlight table into a treemap
It removes the need for a color legend
It changes the aggregation from Sum to Average
questions.explain: Without visible borders, adjacent cells with similar colors can blur together — a border keeps each cell distinct.

questions.q: When do highlight tables and heat maps start to break down as a chart choice?
options: When there are too many rows or columns to fit on screen, or when the measure being colored has no meaningful 'high vs. low'
Whenever more than one dimension is used
They have no meaningful limitations and work for any dataset size
Only when the underlying data source is a live SQL Server connection
questions.explain: These charts depend on a scannable grid and a measure with a meaningful range — too many cells or a measure without a real high/low undermines both.
